title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
premise: Targeted, not an undergraduate sequence. The failure mode of maths-for-ML is spending a year on proofs and never arriving at the machine learning, so every module here ends in something computed by hand on an object from your own work and then checked against a library. You are not being taught to prove theorems. You are being taught to read a paper's equations without skipping them, and to know what an optimiser is actually doing when a training run goes wrong.
why_here: First in Block II and eighth overall, because everything after it — deep learning, transformers from scratch, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning — is unreadable without it, and because nothing in Block I needs it. Block I taught you to build with models. This is where you start understanding them.
laboratory: Your own corpora, because a matrix built from your own data is a fact rather than a textbook exercise. Indie Degree's 203 verified resources make a term-document matrix whose singular values tell you something true about how repetitive your own reading list is. Career Side Quests' scoring pipeline is a real loss function with real variance. The maths lands differently when the matrix is yours.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.
honesty_note: No advanced standing is awarded for this course. Four shipped LLM products evidence nothing about eigendecompositions, and awarding credit for adjacent work would be exactly the self-flattery the programme is built to refuse.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: Mathematics is the one subject where a language model will confidently confirm a wrong derivation that looks like a right one. Judges are instructed to recompute rather than pattern-match, and to score a plausible-looking derivation with a sign error at 0 rather than 2.

items.title: Essence of linear algebra, the geometry
items.locator: Chapters 1–8: vectors, span, linear transformations as matrices, matrix multiplication as composition, and determinants.

items.title: Essence of linear algebra, change of basis and eigenvectors
items.locator: Chapters 9–15: dot products, change of basis, eigenvectors and eigenvalues, abstract vector spaces.

items.title: Linear algebra, written down
items.locator: Chapter 2, Linear Algebra, through 2.7 on linear mappings. The notation, after the geometry — this order round, because the pictures make the symbols readable and not the reverse.

items.title: Matrix decompositions
items.locator: Chapter 4, Matrix Decompositions — eigendecomposition, the singular value decomposition, and 4.6 on low-rank approximation.

items.title: Decompose your own corpus
checkpoints: Term-document matrix built and its shape reported
SVD computed and singular values plotted
Effective rank chosen with a stated threshold
Interpretation written against the actual documents
items.brief: Build a term-document matrix from Indie Degree's own 203 verified resources — titles and notes, no embeddings and no API calls. Compute its SVD with numpy. Report the singular value spectrum, choose an effective rank with a threshold you state before looking, and reconstruct the matrix at that rank. Then do the part that matters: open the top three right singular vectors, read which resources load on each, and say in a sentence what topic each one found. If a component is not interpretable, say that instead of inventing a theme.

items.title: Eigenvectors by hand, then by library
checkpoints: Characteristic polynomial written out for the 3×3
Eigenvalues solved by hand
Eigenvectors solved and normalised
numpy comparison run, and any disagreement explained
items.brief: Take one 2×2 and one 3×3 matrix. Find the eigenvalues by writing out and solving the characteristic polynomial, then find and normalise the eigenvectors — on paper, showing the steps. Verify against numpy.linalg.eig. Where the signs or the ordering differ from yours, explain why that is not a disagreement. Then answer in two sentences: what does it mean that a covariance matrix is symmetric, and what does that guarantee about its eigenvectors.

items.title: Retention: decompositions and what they are for
Essence of calculus, derivatives and the chain rule
items.locator: Chapters 1–6: the derivative as a limit, the power and product rules, and the chain rule.

items.title: Essence of calculus, exponentials and approximation
items.locator: Chapters 7–12: implicit differentiation, limits, exponentials, and Taylor series.

items.title: Vector calculus and backpropagation
items.locator: Chapter 5, Vector Calculus — particularly 5.4 on gradients of matrices and 5.6, which derives backpropagation as repeated application of the chain rule.

items.title: Backpropagation by hand
checkpoints: Forward pass computed by hand with numbers written down
Every partial derivative derived symbolically
Numeric gradients produced for one input
Autograd comparison run and agreement reported to a stated precision
items.brief: Take a two-layer network with three inputs, two hidden units, a sigmoid, and a squared-error loss. Choose concrete weights. Compute the forward pass by hand. Then derive every partial derivative of the loss with respect to every weight symbolically, and evaluate them numerically. Check against PyTorch autograd. Report agreement to a stated number of decimal places, and if anything disagrees, find the sign error rather than adjusting the tolerance.

items.title: Differentiate a loss you actually use
checkpoints: The loss written formally from the code that computes it
Gradient derived with respect to the logits
Result checked numerically
items.brief: Find a loss function in something you have shipped or in a library you depend on, and write it down formally from the source rather than from memory. Derive its gradient with respect to the model's logits. For cross-entropy over a softmax the answer collapses to something famously simple — if you get that, show the cancellation step by step rather than quoting the result.

items.title: Where the chain rule explains the bug
checkpoints: A deep chain constructed and its gradient magnitudes measured per layer
The saturation point identified numerically
A fix applied and re-measured
items.brief: Build a deliberately deep stack of sigmoid layers and measure the gradient magnitude at each layer. Show the decay numerically rather than asserting it. Then explain, from the derivative of the sigmoid itself, why the decay is multiplicative and roughly what factor per layer you should expect. Change one thing — the activation, the initialisation, or a residual connection — and measure again. The claim to defend is which of those you changed and why it was the right one.

items.title: Retention: the chain rule through a graph

modules.title: Probability, and what a loss function is measuring

items.title: Probability and distributions
items.locator: Chapter 6, Probability and Distributions — through 6.5 on Gaussians, and 6.6 on conjugacy and the exponential family.

items.title: Where the model meets the data
items.locator: Chapter 8, When Models Meet Data — 8.1 to 8.3: empirical risk minimisation, parameter estimation, and what maximum likelihood is actually assuming.

items.title: The probabilistic view of a model
items.locator: The lectures on the probabilistic interpretation of least squares and on generalised linear models — where a loss stops being a choice and becomes a consequence of a distributional assumption.

items.title: Cross-entropy is not a choice
checkpoints: The likelihood written for a categorical model
Log taken and negated, with each step justified
The result matched against a library implementation
The Gaussian case derived to squared error
items.brief: Derive cross-entropy from maximum likelihood for a categorical model, showing every step. Then do the same for a Gaussian with fixed variance and arrive at squared error. Write the conclusion in your own words: what distributional assumption are you making every time you reach for MSE, and name one situation in your own work where that assumption is wrong.

items.title: The variance in your own numbers
checkpoints: A real measured set of scores assembled
Bootstrap or analytic interval computed
A previously stated comparison re-examined against the interval
items.brief: Take a set of scores you have actually measured — an eval run, a latency sample, anything with more than thirty observations. Compute a confidence interval, by bootstrap or analytically, and say which you chose and why. Then find a comparison you or someone else has previously stated as a fact — 'X is better than Y' — and check whether the interval supports it. The valuable outcome here is discovering that a difference you believed is inside the noise.

items.title: Retention: likelihood, loss, and what follows from what
Continuous optimisation
items.locator: Chapter 7, Continuous Optimization — gradient descent with momentum, stochastic gradient descent, constrained optimisation and duality.

items.title: Optimisation as it actually behaves in deep networks
items.locator: Chapter 8, Optimization for Training Deep Models — especially 8.2 on the challenges, and 8.5 on adaptive learning rates.

items.title: Three optimisers from their update rules
checkpoints: Plain gradient descent implemented and converging
Momentum added, with the update rule written above the code
Adam implemented including bias correction
All three plotted on the same objective
items.brief: Implement gradient descent, gradient descent with momentum, and Adam in numpy — from the update rules as written in the reading, not from a library and not from memory. Run all three on the same two-dimensional objective with a known minimum, and plot the trajectories. Include Adam's bias-correction terms and then run it once with them removed, so you can show what they actually do in the first few steps.

items.title: Why Adam, and when it is worse
checkpoints: A case constructed where Adam wins, and measured
A case constructed where plain SGD wins, and measured
The mechanism explained from the update rules
items.brief: Construct one objective where Adam clearly beats SGD and one where it clearly does not, and measure both. Then explain the difference from the update rules themselves — what the per-parameter scaling buys you and what it costs. The second case is the point of the assignment: 'use Adam' is the default advice, and a submission that cannot produce a case against it has not understood why it works.

items.title: Make training fail, three ways
checkpoints: Failure by learning rate produced and its signature recorded
Failure by initialisation produced and recorded
Failure by conditioning or scaling produced and recorded
A short diagnostic table written from the three signatures
items.brief: Deliberately break the same training run three ways: a learning rate that diverges, an initialisation that kills the gradient, and inputs on wildly different scales. Record the loss curve and the gradient norms for each. Then write the artifact that makes this worth doing — a short table mapping the symptom you would actually observe to the cause, so that next time you see it in real training you recognise it rather than guessing.

items.title: Retention: optimiser behaviour and failure signatures

modules.title: The mathematics of something you already use

items.title: What a network is computing
items.locator: Chapters 1–2: a layer as a matrix multiplication followed by a nonlinearity, and what the parameters mean.

items.title: Scaled dot-product attention, the equation only
items.locator: Section 3.2.1 and its footnote on why the dot products are scaled. Read this for the mathematics alone; the architecture is AIE-204's job.

items.title: Why the square root of d_k
checkpoints: Variance of a dot product of independent unit-variance vectors derived
The effect on softmax demonstrated numerically at two dimensionalities
The gradient consequence measured
items.brief: The paper justifies dividing by the square root of the key dimension in a single footnote. Derive it: show that the dot product of two independent vectors with unit-variance components has variance equal to the dimension. Then demonstrate numerically what a large-variance input does to softmax, and measure what that does to the gradient. This is the assignment where the whole course pays off — one footnote in a paper you have used for two years, turned into something you can derive.

items.title: The mathematics of one system you built: derivation
checkpoints: System chosen and the mathematical claim stated
The derivation written out
Every claim checked numerically against the running system
items.brief: Pick one component of something you have shipped and write down what it is doing mathematically — the similarity metric in a retrieval path, the scoring function in a pipeline, the aggregation in a ranker. Derive its behaviour rather than describing it, and check each claim against the system as it actually runs. State at least one thing the derivation tells you that you did not know before writing it, or say plainly that it told you nothing new.

items.title: The mathematics of one system you built: publish
checkpoints: Written for a reader who has not seen the system
Notation defined once and used consistently
Published, and linked from the public log
Connected backwards to an earlier chapter's result
items.brief: Publish the derivation as a chapter of the public engineering log. It must stand alone on its own page and must connect backwards to at least one earlier chapter's result. Notation is the thing readers give up on: define it once, use it consistently, and do not switch between index and matrix form without saying so.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your own submissions at defense time, answered aloud without notes and without a calculator. Mathematics is where notes hide the gap most effectively, which is why there are none.
sample_question_shapes: You divided by the square root of d_k. Talk me through the variance argument without writing anything down.
Your gradient check agreed to six decimal places. What would it have looked like if you had a sign error in exactly one weight, and would you have noticed?
You said the difference in your eval numbers was inside the noise. Someone disagrees and says thirty samples is plenty. Answer them.

completion.required: All eleven assignments, both project parts and the defense submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on all four mathematics skills. FSRS then decays them, and this is the course where that matters most — a derivation you cannot reproduce six months later was never knowledge, it was a transcription.
